scenes.narration: Chapter twenty two: designing your own circuits. Knowing how circuits work is one thing. Choosing every part value yourself, from a requirement, is what makes you an engineer. We'll design four real circuits from scratch: a five volt power supply, a transistor switch for a motor, a small audio amplifier, and an L E D blinker. For every part, we'll say why it's that value.
scenes.title: BUILD YOUR OWN CIRCUITS
scenes.subtitle: From a requirement to every part value

scenes.narration: Before building, know your tools. A breadboard: rows of five holes are connected together, and the long rails at the sides carry the supply and ground. A multimeter: voltage across a part, current in series with the circuit, resistance with the power off, and the diode test. An oscilloscope: shows the waveform against time, so you can see ripple, clipping and frequency. And datasheets: always check maximum voltage, current, power and pin order before using a part.

scenes.chapter: Design 1: a 5 V, 500 mA power supply
scenes.narration: Design one: a five volt supply for five hundred milliamps from the mains. Step one, the transformer: the regulator needs about three volts of headroom, plus ripple and diode drops, so aim for about ten volts D C before it. A nine volt r m s transformer gives twelve point seven volts peak, minus one point four for the bridge: eleven point three volts. Step two, the bridge rectifier: four one amp diodes like the one N four double oh one, rated fifty volts or more. Step three, the filter capacitor: for one volt of ripple at five hundred milliamps and a hundred hertz, C equals zero point five over a hundred times one: five thousand microfarads, use four seven hundred or more, rated at least twenty five volts.

Step four, the regulator: a seven eight oh five, which is a refined series regulator, gives a steady five volts. Its heat: eleven point three minus five, times half an amp, about three watts, so it needs a heat sink. Step five, small capacitors at its input and output, a third of a microfarad and a tenth, to keep it stable. And a fuse in the mains side. Every value came from a calculation we learned.

scenes.chapter: Design 2: a transistor switch for a motor
scenes.narration: Design two: a microcontroller pin, five volts, must switch a twelve volt motor drawing two hundred milliamps. Choose an N P N transistor rated for well over two hundred milliamps, like the B C three three seven, with a minimum beta of about a hundred. For a solid switch we want saturation, so give it more base current than needed: needed is two hundred over a hundred, two milliamps; use five times more, ten milliamps. Base resistor: five minus zero point seven, over ten milliamps, four thirty ohms. Use four seventy. And across the motor, a flyback diode, because the motor is an inductor.

The design numbers. Load current two hundred milliamps. Minimum beta one hundred, so at least two milliamps of base current. Overdrive by five times for hard saturation: ten milliamps. R B equals four point three over ten milliamps, four thirty ohms, standard four seventy. Transistor heat when on: zero point two volts times zero point two amps, forty milliwatts. And the one N four double oh one flyback diode across the motor, pointing to the twelve volt rail.
scenes.title: SWITCH DESIGN

scenes.narration: Design three: amplify a ten millivolt microphone signal about a hundred times, from a twelve volt supply. A common emitter stage with voltage divider bias. Step one, pick the current: about two milliamps. Step two, put the emitter at about ten percent of the supply, around two volts: R E equals two volts over two milliamps, one kilohm. Step three, put the collector halfway between the emitter and the supply for the biggest swing: R C about two kilohms. Step four, the divider: the base must sit at two point seven volts; with beta times R E at a hundred k, keep R two under ten k: thirty three k and ten k. Step five, the gain: r e is thirteen point four ohms, so with R E bypassed, R C over r e is about one fifty. Exactly the amplifier we built in chapter sixteen.

Step six, the capacitors for audio down to twenty hertz. Input impedance about one point one k, so the coupling capacitor needs under a hundred and fourteen ohms at twenty hertz: a hundred microfarads. The bypass must be below r e at twenty hertz: six hundred and eighty microfarads. And a hundred nanofarad decoupling capacitor at the supply pin. Now you can design an amplifier from nothing but a requirement.

scenes.narration: Design four: blink an L E D about once a second, with a five five five. For a one hertz astable with roughly equal on and off times, make R one small and R two large. Choose C equals ten microfarads. Then f equals one point four four over R one plus two R two, times C. For one hertz: R one plus two R two equals one hundred and forty four kilohms. Choose R one equals four point seven k and R two equals sixty eight k: f equals one point four four over one forty point seven k times ten micro, about one point zero two hertz. The L E D resistor: five minus two, over fifteen milliamps, two hundred ohms, use two twenty.

The numbers once more. C ten microfarads. R one four point seven k, R two sixty eight k. High time: zero point six nine three times seventy two point seven k times ten micro, zero point five zero seconds. Low time: zero point six nine three times sixty eight k times ten micro, zero point four seven seconds. About one blink per second. You've just designed four complete circuits.
scenes.title: BLINKER DESIGN

scenes.narration: Recap. Every design starts from a requirement and uses the formulas we learned. Power supply: transformer, bridge, capacitor for ripple, regulator with headroom and a heat sink. Switch: overdrive the base for saturation, add a flyback diode. Amplifier: choose the current, put V E near ten percent and V C midway, size the divider and the capacitors. Timer: pick C, then solve for the resistors. Next, the final placement revision.
